newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin claims diplomatic wins as economy stalls.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin claims diplomatic wins as economy stalls.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin boasted on Tuesday that he had gathered a rich diplomatic harvest in May but stormclouds loomed over Russia's sickly economy, where the government scaled back earlier forecasts of a return to growth this year.
"All in all May was a striking month for Russia," the president told First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais in remarks clearly aimed at the attendant cameraman.

"Look at how many problems we managed to resolve in May. Chechnya - a treaty, Belarus - a treaty, Ukraine - a treaty, NATO in Paris - a treaty, all that in May. I would say it was clearly a month of a super harvest," Yeltsin added.

Confined to bed at the beginning of this year, the Kremlin leader has pushed himself hard to make up for eight months of illness, flying to and from foreign capitals and hosting a series of visiting dignitaries in the Kremlin.
He has also pushed his officials, forcing the pace in some of Russia's toughest post-communist dipomatic battles and declaring victories one by one.
On Tuesday he intervened in Russia's economic problems, pressing the opposition-dominated parliament to pass tax reform and budget cutting bills within three weeks.
The Russian government confirmed a downward revision of its economic forecasts on Tuesday, pointing to lower output, lower gross domestic product (GDP) and lower investment this year.

Government figures distributed at the State Duma lower house of parliament showed that industrial output and GDP could fall by up to two percent in 1997, while agricultural output and investment could be five percent below 1996 levels.
Chubais, meanwhile, heralded a new political storm by issuing a tacit threat to the parliament that it might face dissolution and fresh elections if it did not back the bills.

"We cannot wait, the economy and the people cannot wait. That's why we have such a tough position," Chubais said in an interview with the Kommersant business newspaper in which he hinted that Yeltsin was ready to carry out the threat.

Yeltsin's communist and nationalist opponents, generally hostile to spending cuts, have also attacked the partnership deal he signed with NATO as a capitulation to the West, which plans to expand its defence alliance towards the borders of the defunct Soviet superpower.

But liberals say the NATO deal made the best of a bad job and there as been less criticism of the treaties signed with ex-Soviet republics Ukraine and Belarus, which have helped Moscow improve relations with its Slav neighbours.

In the hundred days since he declared himself "fully fit" Yeltsin also announced a "strategic partnership" with China and boosted ties with India and Japan, which then dropped objections to Moscow joining the Group of Seven leading industrial nations.
Yeltsin, declared fit to travel by the chief Kremlin doctor on Monday, is now looking forward to next month's Denver G-7 meeting, where he expects the group to be transformed into the G-8.

Analysts, used to complaining that Russia appears to have no foreign policy, do not all agree on the effectiveness of the deals, but several said they had increased Russia's security and all were clearly impressed by the pace.

"These are real achievements in Russia's foreign policy. In...reinforcing its legal status in the East, in the West in the near abroad (former Soviet Union)," said Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy head of Russia's USA and Canada Institute.
"It's been very active, very dramatic," laughed Andrei Piontkowsky, from the Moscow Centre for Strategic Studies.
But Piontkowsky warned in a telephone interview that Yeltsin needed to apply the same sort of effort closer to home if he was to consolidate his foreign policy gains.
